title: Trump orders US military not to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa for now
content:
President Donald Trump on Monday ordered the Army not to move ahead with plans to detonate five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa unless a federal court and the state's incoming governor agreed.
Late on Monday, a court partly cleared the way, ruling the military could proceed with its plans to detonate the lead azide, a highly volatile compound that is reportedly at risk of exploding on its own.
The possible detonation has faced legal challenges and public outcry over potential health and environmental hazards.
In announcing his order, Trump said the US had "an opportunity to do a highly controlled detonation of these dangerous and rapidly corroding materials" because the weather is optimal.
"I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward," Trump said, referring to the federal appeals court.
He added that he was "making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation".
Sand, a Democrat who will not lead the state until January, has not said whether he agreed with the military's plan. The current governor of the state is Republican Kim Reynolds.
Before the court ruling, Sand urged the Trump administration to be transparent and share information publicly that he's received in private briefings. He said Iowans are entitled to know how they "came to this situation" and why "this is the best path forward".
A court had ordered a pause on the plan after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, which was originally scheduled for last Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown.
Even after the pause was put in place, the justice department told the court that the Army intended to move forward because of an "immediate risk" that the munitions could "spontaneously explode".
Environmental groups have accused the federal government of skirting the judicial process.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move it, according to Iowa Public Radio.
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says no level of lead exposure is considered safe. Lead exposure through inhalation or ingestion can pose serious health risks to humans and animals, particularly children.
The 8th Circuit US Court of Appeals said in its order on Monday night that the EPA adequately included safeguards in the emergency permit to minimise dust dispersal to address safety concerns.
The US Army has said it planned to carry out the detonation on Wednesday to allow for "optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced". It's unclear whether that plan will change.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, has argued it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Middletown's Mayor Rodney Johnson on Monday backed the detonation and said it "must take place".
"It doesn't matter who dropped the ball on the removal of these expired munitions, the ball is now in November 2026 Court," Johnson said in a statement. "The buzzer is ticking and if we don't take this opportunity to Safely dispose of the problem, then actual lives may be at stake !!!"
He added that "every possible precaution" had been put into place to ensure people's safety.
The government has argued that, because this is an event that requires immediate action, the Army can move forward without a permit for detonation.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive, category-specific development (the US military's plan to detonate toxic explosives in Iowa) and provides a clear reason for readers to care (public health and environmental hazards).

title: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling
content:
The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that the country had carried out genocide against the Rohingya minority – marking the first time a state has been found guilty of the crime .
A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma.
The UK is joined by several other countries in acknowledging the ICJ ruling, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and Canada.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values and must be matched by clear action."
The senior military leaders facing sanctions are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo.
Miliband added that Myanmar's President Min Aung Hlaing , who was sanctioned by the UK in 2021, is "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" as he was head of the military at the time of the genocide in 2017.
He said: "Myanmar must stop ongoing violations, investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators, and prevent such an atrocity from ever happening again."
Miliband also called for an "immediate pause in hostilities to enable humanitarian aid to get through, a stop to air strikes on civilians, and the release of political prisoners, as well as dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement".
The foreign secretary confirmed that new legislation would be passed to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country, which was known as Burma until 1989.
Last week, he expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the ICJ ruled the country had committed genocide during the brutal military campaign in 2017.
He told MPs on Monday the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, and there would be a dedicated meeting in a fortnight.
The court found on Thursday that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence" it had seen.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world. The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention .
In its ruling last week, the court determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were murdered during the clearance operation in the western Rakhine state that borders Bangladesh and the Bay of Bengal. Myanmar denied the claims against it.
Reports said that entire villages were burnt down, and that women and girls were raped.
Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and were being supported by Bangladesh.
Myanmar's leader during the genocide, Aung San Suu Kyi , was deposed by the military in 2021.
MPs heard that air strikes and violence from the Arakan army were still happening.
ranking_reason: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling

analysis.reason: UK sanctions top Myanmar military leaders after Rohingya genocide ruling

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant development in international relations, detailing the UK's response to the International Court of Justice's ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. The article provides concrete information on the UK's sanctions and diplomatic efforts, and highlights the gravity of the situation and the need for action.

title: Andrew received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told
content:
A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a £750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.
Nebahat Isbilen is alleging her former business adviser, Selman Turk, misappropriated £38m of her assets, including a payment to the then-Duke of York which she believed was for help with her passport.
Turk has rejected the allegations, saying the 81-year-old Isbilen knew the money was actually being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, a politician who is in prison in Turkey.
Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the £750,000 and is expected to give evidence to the High Court in December. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.
Isbilen's lawyers also told the court on Monday that Turk had instructed a separate £15,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor's ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, purportedly for the former Duchess of York's 60th birthday party in 2019, and an unquantified  "wedding gift" payment for their daughter Princess Beatrice.
Isbilen's family founded a major soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.
But when her husband, Ilhan, a former member of the Turkish parliament, was arrested in 2015, she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Her lawyers said the charges were "politically motivated" and that in 2017 she was facing "political persecution".
She left Turkey for Greece in 2017 and moved to London in 2018.
Simon Colton KC, representing Isbilen, said she met Turk in January 2017 and gave him control of most of her financial assets.
But Turk "deliberately and systematically abused" her trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, Colton added.
Colton added that Isbilen approved the £750,000 payment to Andrew, but that Turk "lied to her" about its purpose, which was "a further example of his dishonesty".
The court heard that Isbilen had a private dinner with the then Duke and Duchess of York at Turk's flat in December 2019 where she discussed her husband's case.
Turk's lawyers told the court that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own affairs.
Joshua Hitchens, representing Turk, said in written submissions: "In circumstances where the claimant dined with the duke and duchess and discussed her husband with them, she cannot have believed that the £750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa."
The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

final_quality.reason: This article reports a significant development in a high-profile legal case involving a member of the British royal family, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. The case is notable for its international political and financial implications, and the article provides clear and concise information about the allegations and evidence presented in court. The story is newsworthy and has significant public interest value.
